sheets.title: Systematic arithmetic extensions after four basic operations; no entrance test
sheets.body: **MAT-ARITH — arithmetic extensions, learned in subskills.** Start with START-01 fraction meaning/equivalence, then follow the arithmetic-bridge rows above. Original practice: (1) draw and compare 1/2,2/4,3/4 with equal reference wholes; (2) calculate 1/3+1/6, (2/3)×(3/4), (3/4)÷(1/2), stating nonzero-denominator conditions; (3) connect 1/4,0.25,25% and distinguish 2:3 from a fraction of the total; (4) add/subtract/multiply/divide simple negative numbers and explain order on a number line; (5) compare 2+3×4,(2+3)×4,−(2²),(−2)²; (6) learn zero/negative powers, roots and scientific notation from the explicit row; (7) after percent changes are taught, calculate a 12% decrease followed by a 12% increase and explain its base; (8) learn milli as one thousandth, convert 2.5 milliseconds to seconds, and estimate the count in an hour; (9) later distinguish rational from irrational representation and exact from finite-precision values. These are teaching tasks, not evidence already achieved or an admission test. Do not assume any extension from four-operation fluency.

sheets.title: Elementary→intermediate algebra, equality/inequality and domain progression
sheets.body: **MAT-ALG — algebra in levels.** Start with (1) translate “three groups of x and two more” into an expression, evaluate it at two values, and distinguish an expression from an equation; (2) solve x+6=13 and 4x=20 by doing the same valid operation to both sides, then check by substitution. Next learn (3) expand 3(x+2) and compare it with 3x+2 using a counterexample; (4) solve 2(3x−1)=4x+10; (5) solve −2x+3>9 and explain sign reversal. Later, when intermediate algebra is active, (6) factor x²−5x+6 and solve its zero equation; (7) simplify (x²−1)/(x−1) with its original domain; (8) solve (x−2)/(x+1)>0 with exclusions. Do not require items 6–8 before beginning functions, programming or simple prediction.

sheets.title: Concentration and adaptive-selection limits
sheets.body:
**MAT-BOUND — learning theory.** (1) Apply a bounded independent-variable concentration inequality with explicit assumptions. (2) Explain how a union bound changes when selecting among finitely many models. (3) Construct a data-leakage/adaptive-testing counterexample to an unjustified independence assumption. Focus on whether the theorem applies, not just substituting numbers.

**MAT-BOUND enhancement.** In addition to the existing sheet, derive Markov's inequality for nonnegative variables and Chebyshev from it; apply Hoeffding only under its bounded independent-sample assumptions. Compare a single-model bound with a finite union bound and an adaptively selected score. Distinguish expectations, high-probability guarantees and empirical confidence procedures. This is concentration literacy before advanced empirical-process theory.

sheets.title: Functions before later exponential/logarithm depth
sheets.body: **MAT-LOG — functions, exponents and logarithms.** (1) For f(x)=2x+1, evaluate f(0),f(3), state an input/output rule and distinguish f(x) from f×x. (2) Compose f with g(x)=x² and compare the two orders. (3) Derive exponential laws for positive bases and explain which extensions need conditions. (4) For f(x)=ln(2x+1), give the real domain and inverse. (5) Refute ln(a+b)=ln a+ln b with positive a,b and justify ln(ab)=ln a+ln b under valid conditions. Start items 1–2 before items 3–5.

sheets.title: Taylor approximation, error conditions, Jacobian/Hessian
sheets.body: **MAT-TAYLOR — Taylor approximation, Jacobians, Hessians and error.** (1) For exp(x), derive its degree-two polynomial at zero and a Lagrange-form remainder; for |x|≤a, bound the absolute remainder by exp(a)a³/6 under the needed differentiability. Evaluate the bound at x=0.1 and compare with actual error. (2) For f(x,y)=x²+xy+3y², derive gradient and Hessian; write the second-order Taylor expression about a point and show it is exact. (3) For a vector-valued map, state the Jacobian's input/output dimensions; distinguish a Hessian of a scalar function from a Jacobian. State conditions before exchanging derivatives or invoking an error theorem. MML Ch.5/selected MIT 18.02SC supports the calculus; full real analysis is not the first lesson.

Compute E[X|Y=0], E[X|Y=1], and verify E[E[X|Y]]=E[X]. (2) After basic integration, transform X uniform on (0,1) to Y=X²; derive the support/density, including the inverse derivative, and check normalization. (3) After Jacobians, transform uniform (X,Y) on the unit square by U=X+Y,V=X−Y; derive the image region and absolute inverse-Jacobian determinant. Distinguish probability mass, density, conditional expectation and a point estimate.

sheets.title: Numerical/Bellman fixed-point reasoning and limits
sheets.body: **MAT-FIX — fixed points and their different meanings.** (1) Find the fixed point of g(x)=(x+2)/3 and compute iterations from x₀=0. Show contraction factor 1/3 and bound |xₙ−x*|. (2) Give a map with a fixed point but divergent iteration from some starts, such as g(x)=2x. (3) When studying finite discounted MDPs, prove the Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction in the sup norm for 0≤γ<1 and bounded rewards. Existence, uniqueness and convergence are separate assertions with assumptions. Logical fixed-point/self-reference results in C09/C17 are a later, different topic; a numerical contraction is not a Gödel-machine theorem.

sheets.title: Monte Carlo, importance weights/support and uncertainty
sheets.body: **MAT-MC — Monte Carlo and importance sampling.** Let p=(0.2,0.3,0.5), h=(0,1,4), and proposal q=(0.5,0.25,0.25). (1) Calculate the exact expectation. (2) Estimate it from IID p samples and report Monte Carlo variability without inventing runs. (3) Derive the ordinary importance estimator using p/q and check its expectation exactly under q. (4) Replace q by a proposal missing positive-p support and explain failure. (5) Compare ordinary with self-normalized importance sampling: the latter is generally biased at finite sample size; consistency/variance require conditions. Treat effective-sample-size summaries as diagnostics, not automatic confidence guarantees. Begin with finite cases; continuous integrals enter after M05.

sheets.title: ELBO/posterior-KL and amortized inference
sheets.body: **MAT-VI — variational and amortized inference.** A model assigns p(x,z=0)=0.1 and p(x,z=1)=0.3 for the observed x. With q(z)=(0.5,0.5), compute evidence, posterior, ELBO=E_q[log p(x,z)−log q(z)] and KL(q||p(z|x)); verify log p(x)=ELBO+KL under valid support/finite-value conditions. Repeat using q equal to the posterior. Explain approximation-family bias versus sampling/optimization error and how q_φ(z|x) shares inference across inputs. Use the [Blei–Kucukelbir–McAuliffe review](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.00670) only for the relevant definitions/ELBO section, not as an additional full-paper reproduction obligation.

sheets.title: Computability/reductions/complexity
sheets.body: **ALG-TCS — TCS and feasibility.** (1) Explain recognizer versus decider with a halting example. (2) Prove one simple reduction: a decider for program equivalence would decide whether a program halts, using a carefully specified construction or a suitably restricted equivalent formulation. State semantic assumptions. (3) Distinguish polynomial time in numeric magnitude from bit length using subset sum. (4) State P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete correctly; a problem being NP-hard does not establish that no practical structured instances can be solved. (5) Explain how exponential search, uncomputability and implementation inefficiency are different obstacles.

sheets.title: Typed-DSL synthesis and constraint-guided search
sheets.body:
**ALG-SYN — program synthesis.** Define a finite typed DSL with constants, input variables, addition and multiplication with an explicit size limit. Enumerate programs fitting a few integer examples; canonicalize or track equivalent candidates to avoid obvious duplicates. Hold out both input values and task families. Construct two programs fitting the training examples but disagreeing elsewhere, then choose a discriminating query. Compare a plain search with a stated reuse/prior scheme under a matched evaluation budget. This is a toy synthesis experiment, not a reproduction of DreamCoder's full empirical results.

**ALG-SYN enhancement — DSL, SAT/SMT and counterexamples.** For the existing bounded typed arithmetic DSL, distinguish syntactic programs, denotational behavior on inputs, search order/prior and an examples-consistent version space. Translate a small finite constraint into Boolean conditions and enumerate a truth table. Then inspect one official [Z3 logical-modeling example](https://microsoft.github.io/z3guide/docs/logic/intro/) or an equivalent locally checked solver task. Compare enumeration with constraint-guided candidate search under the same candidate/evaluation budget. A returned model must be checked against the original examples; additional examples should discriminate remaining candidate programs. Do not claim that a timeout proves absence of a solution.

sheets.title: Specifications, SAT/SMT and trusted-base limits
sheets.body:
**ALG-VERIFY — specification and verification.** Specify pre/postconditions for binary search, prove the loop invariant and termination, and identify the assumptions the proof needs (sorted order, immutable input, integer indexing). Add property-based tests on small generated arrays and compare to a simple linear oracle. Distinguish finite tests, mathematical proof, proof-assistant checking and the trusted implementation/runtime. A formal proof applies to its model, not automatically to every compiled execution.

**ALG-VERIFY enhancement — formal verification and solver semantics.** Over integer x, encode 0≤x≤2 and x>1; verify a satisfying model by substitution. Add x<1 and explain unsatisfiability. Distinguish integers from reals and bounded machine integers, `sat` from `unsat` from `unknown`, and a proof/counterexample about an encoding from correctness of the original intended program. Write pre/postconditions and a small loop invariant, then compare an exhaustive finite oracle, unit tests and a mathematical proof. Solver libraries are optional for this first finite example; no installation or platform build is required. Later logical fixed-point/diagonal reasoning belongs to the computability/RSI branch, not numerical fixed-point iteration.

sheets.title: Aggregate/potential analysis and cost models
sheets.body: **ALG-AMORT — worst-case, expected and amortized work.** Start a dynamic array at capacity 1. On an append to a full array, allocate twice the capacity, copy existing entries, then append. (1) List capacity and actual copies for the first 10 appends. (2) Bound total copies over n appends by summing the geometric growth sizes, and include ordinary writes. (3) Prove O(1) amortized append by an aggregate or valid potential argument. (4) Explain why one append can cost Θ(n), why no random input assumption is needed, and why an expected hash-table bound is a different statement. Add a divide-and-conquer recurrence and a greedy exchange argument only as the selected algorithm demands. Use MAT-REC for generating functions, not a calculus entrance gate.

(5) Define a grammar for balanced parentheses and explain why its recognition problem differs from the finite automaton example. (6) Connect recognizer/decider, Turing-complete computation and reductions only when that theoretical depth is active. Python's [tutorial functions/control flow](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html) and [data structures](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html) are the initial source; MIT 6.045J supplies selected formal-language topics later. sheets.title: Finite MDP/value/TD/planning worksheet, now defined
sheets.body: **RL-R1 — finite MDPs, values, tabular TD and planning.** This resolves the baseline's undefined R1 locator. (1) Specify a finite discounted MDP: state/action sets, transition probabilities, rewards, initial/terminal conditions, objective and 0≤γ<1. (2) In a one-state/one-action process with reward 2 each step and γ=1/2, derive v=2+v/2 and solve it; iterate T(v)=2+v/2 from v₀=0 and relate error to contraction. (3) In a separate observed transition with current estimate v(s)=1, next estimate v(s')=3, reward 2, γ=1/2 and step size α=0.2, hand-compute one TD(0) update using the old values. For a terminal next state use the declared zero continuation value. (4) Compare exact finite-state Bellman solutions, sampled Monte Carlo returns and tabular TD under a fixed data budget; quantify variability from actual executions. (5) Add a learned table model and a fixed number of planning updates; deliberately bias the model and test real-environment performance versus model-predicted utility. No RNN, Transformer or full convex-optimization course is needed. Neural function approximation/off-policy instability comes later in L19. sheets.title: Generative objective evidence
sheets.body: **ML-GEN — generative objective.** On a finite distribution, specify valid probabilities, compute a normalized likelihood and sample from it. Then reconstruct one latent/generative objective (MAT-VI supplies a tiny ELBO) or one diffusion objective only when needed. Separate density/sample quality from learned representation utility and downstream task evaluation. One selected method suffices; do not complete GAN, VAE, every diffusion family and video generation as a cumulative common-core gate.

sheets.title: Separate SSL representation evidence
sheets.body: **ML-SSL — independent representation evidence.** Define a prediction/contrastive target or two data views with explicit augmentations and label/data provenance. Compare the representation with a random/simple baseline under a matched training/evaluation budget. Include a collapsed/constant representation as a diagnostic and a held-out downstream or transfer test using only training-derived preprocessing. State which augmentations are scientifically valid and what information they remove. Do not treat “trained without labels,” a low pretext loss, generative likelihood or a guided implementation as full SSL mastery. Pick one objective from D039–040; no new mandatory paper reproduction is added.

sheets.title: SFT/reward/preference/DPO/RL distinctions
sheets.body: **ML-POST — SFT, rewards and preferences.** (1) Define a tiny instruction/response task and train/evaluate splits; identify which tokens an SFT loss should include. (2) For a preferred/dispreferred response pair, model preference as σ(r_w−r_l), derive its negative log likelihood and explain why a learned reward may exploit length/style or label artifacts. (3) For β>0 and a fixed reference policy, derive the DPO loss −log σ(β[(log π(y_w|x)−log π_ref(y_w|x))−(log π(y_l|x)−log π_ref(y_l|x))]); state support, sequence/masking and preference-model assumptions rather than treating it as a universal truth. (4) Compare outcome correctness, held-out preference accuracy and distribution shift; no public-test tuning. (5) Only if a research question needs RL post-training, extend to policy-gradient/actor-critic/PPO/GRPO after L18–L20 and report the extra sampling/compute. D054–056 and the inspected TensorTonic SFT/preference examples provide practice. The relevant sections of [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155) or [DPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290) are targeted method references, not two additional compulsory reproductions.

sheets.title: Verifier-guided reasoning and matched-budget evaluation
sheets.body: **ML-VERIFY — verifier-guided reasoning.** Use a finite arithmetic/DSL task family with a known checked oracle. Distinguish final-answer correctness from validity of intermediate steps, process supervision from outcome supervision, and a true finite verifier from a learned reward/judge. Compare a baseline generator/search, a verifier/reranker and one controlled variant with equal candidate/token/compute budgets and untouched task families. Introduce a faulty/permissive verifier to detect reward hacking or evaluator exploitation. Report search coverage, valid solutions, false acceptance, costs and ambiguous/no-solution/timeout cases separately. A learned judge's agreement is not a proof. [Let's Verify Step by Step](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050) is an optional targeted comparison of supervision choices; do not import its headline results into the toy study.
